lead: An equalizer is a receiver filter that cancels the ISI a real channel leaves behind. It keeps the last few received samples on a tapped delay line, multiplies them by adjustable weights and adds them, so that at each sampling instant the wanted symbol comes out with little spill from its neighbours. The zero-forcing equalizer solves for the weights that force the ISI to zero at chosen instants. The adaptive equalizer learns its weights from a known training sequence and then from its own decisions. DSL modems and mobile receivers all contain one.
prereq: You need: ISI and the Nyquist criterion (the sampled overall pulse and peak distortion).

blocks.text: A channel smears each pulse over several symbol periods. At the sampling instants the smear is described by the samples h<sub>m</sub> of the received pulse at t = mT: h<sub>0</sub> is the wanted height, and h<sub>−1</sub>, h<sub>1</sub>, h<sub>2</sub>, … are the precursor and postcursor ISI. The received sample sequence is x(n) = Σ<sub>m</sub> h<sub>m</sub> a(n − m) + noise.
A linear transversal equalizer is a delay line with taps T apart, weights c−N … cN and one adder. With 2N + 1 taps its output is
Here c<sub>k</sub> is the weight on tap k and x(n − k) is the sample held on that tap; the centre tap c<sub>0</sub> holds the sample being decided.

The channel and equalizer in cascade have the combined sampled response v<sub>m</sub> = Σ<sub>k</sub> c<sub>k</sub> h<sub>m−k</sub>, the convolution of the two sequences. Zero ISI means v<sub>0</sub> = 1 and v<sub>m</sub> = 0 for every m ≠ 0. The equalizer sits after the receive filter and before the decision device (the slicer).
A zero-forcing (ZF) equalizer with 2N + 1 taps forces v0 = 1 and vm = 0 for m = ±1, …, ±N. That is 2N + 1 linear equations in 2N + 1 unknowns:
Σk ck hm−k = 1 for m = 0, and 0 for m = ±1 … ±N
Here in matrix form H·c = [0 … 0 1 0 … 0]ᵀ, where row m of H holds h<sub>m+N</sub> … h<sub>m−N</sub>. Solve by elimination or by inverting H.

A finite equalizer cannot null everything: the zeros are forced only for |m| ≤ N, and new, smaller ISI appears at m = ±(N + 1) and beyond. The first worked example shows this. With unlimited taps the ZF equalizer becomes C(f) = 1/H(f): the inverse of the channel.

The price is noise enhancement. Where |H(f)| is small, |C(f)| = 1/|H(f)| is large, and noise at those frequencies is amplified with the signal. For white noise samples the equalizer multiplies the noise variance by Σ ck². At a spectral null (H(f) = 0) the ZF equalizer would need infinite gain. The minimum mean-square error (MMSE) equalizer avoids this by minimising the total power of ISI plus noise instead of forcing ISI to zero.

sections.h3: Adaptive equalizer: learn the taps with LMS

blocks.text: A ZF design needs the channel samples, which are unknown at start-up and drift. An adaptive equalizer starts from simple weights (centre tap 1, others 0) and updates them after every symbol. The usual rule is the least mean square (LMS) algorithm:

Here μ is the step size (a small positive number), x(n − k) is the sample on tap k and e(n) = d(n) − y(n) is the error between the desired symbol d(n) and the equalizer output y(n) taken before the slicer.

items: Training mode. The transmitter first sends a sequence the receiver already knows, so d(n) is the known training symbol.

Decision-directed mode. After training, d(n) is the slicer's decision â(n), and e(n) = â(n) − y(n). The error is not zero, because y(n) is the analogue value before the slicer, for example 0.93 when â(n) = +1.
Step size. A large μ converges fast but the taps jitter; a small μ settles closer but tracks changes slowly.

blocks.text: Each update steps the taps down the slope of e²(n). Over many symbols LMS approaches the MMSE setting, not the ZF one. Figure 5.3.1 shows the three-tap equalizer of the first worked example and the response before and after it.

examples.question: A channel has sampled response h<sub>−1</sub> = 0.2, h<sub>0</sub> = 1, h<sub>1</sub> = 0.3, all other h<sub>m</sub> = 0. Design a three-tap zero-forcing equalizer (c<sub>−1</sub>, c<sub>0</sub>, c<sub>1</sub>). Find the equalized response v<sub>m</sub> for m = −2 … 2 and the peak distortion before and after. By what factor does the equalizer multiply white noise power?
steps: m = +1: c<sub>−1</sub>(0) + c<sub>0</sub>(0.3) + c<sub>1</sub>(1) = 0, so c<sub>1</sub> = −0.3c<sub>0</sub>.
New ISI outside the forced range: v<sub>−2</sub> = c<sub>−1</sub>h<sub>−1</sub> = −0.2273 × 0.2 = −0.0455 and v<sub>2</sub> = c<sub>1</sub>h<sub>1</sub> = −0.3409 × 0.3 = −0.1023.
Noise gain Σc<sub>k</sub>² = 0.2273² + 1.1364² + 0.3409² = 0.0517 + 1.2913 + 0.1162 = 1.459, so the noise power rises by 1.459 times (1.64 dB).
examples.answer: c = (−0.2273, 1.1364, −0.3409); v = (−0.0455, 0, 1, 0, −0.1023); peak distortion falls from 0.5 to 0.148, at a noise power cost of 1.459 times.

examples.question: The same channel is equalized adaptively by LMS in training mode with μ = 0.1 and starting taps (c<sub>−1</sub>, c<sub>0</sub>, c<sub>1</sub>) = (0, 1, 0). The training symbols are a(0) … a(5) = +1, +1, −1, +1, +1, −1 and there is no noise. Do the updates at n = 2 and n = 3.
steps: The squared error fell from 0.25 to 0.0099, and every tap has moved towards the zero-forcing signs (negative, above 1, negative).
examples.answer: After two updates c = (−0.0341, 1.0340, −0.0600); the errors were −0.5 and 0.0995.

traps: Mixing h<sub>m</sub> and c<sub>k</sub>. h<sub>m</sub> are channel samples, c<sub>k</sub> are equalizer taps; the combined response is their convolution v<sub>m</sub> = Σ c<sub>k</sub>h<sub>m−k</sub>.
Claiming a finite ZF equalizer removes all ISI. It forces zeros only for |m| ≤ N; new ISI appears just outside, as v<sub>±2</sub> in the worked example.
Forgetting noise enhancement. ZF has large gain where |H(f)| is small; it is not the best choice at low SNR, where MMSE wins.
Taking the error after the slicer. In decision-directed mode e(n) = â(n) − y(n) uses the analogue output y(n); using the decision on both sides would make e = 0 and stop adaptation.

quiz.q: Write the frequency-domain condition for an infinitely long zero-forcing equalizer.
quiz.a: C(f)H(f) = 1, so C(f) = 1/H(f), where H(f) is the channel response and C(f) the equalizer response.

quiz.q: Why does a zero-forcing equalizer amplify noise near a spectral null?
quiz.a: There |H(f)| is small, so |C(f)| = 1/|H(f)| is large and the noise at those frequencies is amplified with the signal. At H(f) = 0 infinite gain would be needed.

quiz.q: A channel has h<sub>0</sub> = 1, h<sub>1</sub> = 0.4 and all other samples zero. Find a two-tap equalizer (c<sub>0</sub>, c<sub>1</sub>) that forces v<sub>0</sub> = 1 and v<sub>1</sub> = 0, and the residual v<sub>2</sub>.
quiz.a: v<sub>0</sub> = c<sub>0</sub>h<sub>0</sub> = 1 gives c<sub>0</sub> = 1. v<sub>1</sub> = c<sub>0</sub>h<sub>1</sub> + c<sub>1</sub>h<sub>0</sub> = 0.4 + c<sub>1</sub> = 0 gives c<sub>1</sub> = −0.4. v<sub>2</sub> = c<sub>1</sub>h<sub>1</sub> = −0.16.

quiz.q: An LMS tap has c<sub>k</sub>(n) = 0.3, μ = 0.01, e(n) = 0.2 and x(n − k) = 0.5. Find c<sub>k</sub>(n + 1).
In decision-directed mode, why can a short burst of decision errors stop an adaptive equalizer from recovering?
quiz.a: Wrong decisions give wrong errors e(n), so LMS moves the taps in a wrong direction. That raises the ISI, which causes more wrong decisions, and the loop can lock into a bad setting. Receivers then fall back to training.

quiz.q: Why is an MMSE equalizer preferred to zero-forcing at low SNR?
quiz.a: MMSE minimises ISI power plus noise power together, so it accepts a little residual ISI rather than a large noise gain. At low SNR the noise term dominates, so ZF's noise enhancement costs more than the ISI it removes.

beyond: Decision-feedback equalizers subtract the postcursor ISI of past decisions instead of filtering it, and fractionally spaced equalizers use taps closer than T to become insensitive to the sampling phase; both are standard in high-speed serial links. The LMS rule is the same stochastic gradient descent that trains neural networks. Search for decision feedback equalizer, fractionally spaced equalizer and normalised LMS.

figure.caption: The worked example's three-tap equalizer. It forces v<sub>±1</sub> = 0 exactly, but leaves small new ISI at m = ±2 (−0.045 and −0.102), so the peak distortion falls from 0.5 to 0.148 rather than to zero.
